cls: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) - propionic acid derivative
quick: Immediate-release 50-75 mg 3-4 times daily; extended-release 200 mg once daily (max 300 mg/day IR)
Take with food, milk or antacid to reduce GI upset
Avoid, especially from 30 weeks (third trimester) - risk to fetal heart/kidneys
Use with caution; small amounts in milk - short-term low dose preferred
Avoid in significant renal impairment; can reduce renal perfusion
Caution in hepatic impairment; consider dose reduction and monitor
Renal function, blood pressure, GI symptoms, hemoglobin, LFTs
summary: Ketoprofen is a propionic-acid NSAID with analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic effects, used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and pain. It works by inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase and reducing prostaglandin synthesis. Like all NSAIDs it carries boxed warnings for serious cardiovascular thrombotic events and gastrointestinal bleeding/ulceration, and is contraindicated around coronary artery bypass graft surgery.
indications: Management of the signs and symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis
Management of the signs and symptoms of osteoarthritis
Relief of mild to moderate pain (immediate-release)

dosage.d: 50-75 mg three to four times daily

dosage.n: Use lowest effective dose with monitoring

admin: Take with food, milk or an antacid to reduce stomach upset
Swallow extended-release capsules whole - do not crush or chew
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration
Maintain hydration and avoid in the perioperative CABG period
moa: Ketoprofen inhibits cyclo-oxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), reducing the synthesis of prostaglandins that mediate inflammation, pain, and fever. It may also have some lipoxygenase-inhibiting and lysosomal-membrane-stabilising activity. The reduction in protective prostaglandins underlies its gastrointestinal and renal adverse effects.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to ketoprofen, aspirin or other NSAIDs (including aspirin-induced asthma/urticaria)
Setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery
Active gastrointestinal bleeding or peptic ulceration

preg: Avoid, particularly from around 30 weeks gestation, due to risk of premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus, oligohydramnios, and fetal renal impairment. Use in the first and second trimesters only if clearly necessary and at the lowest dose for the shortest time.
lact: Small amounts are excreted in breast milk. Short-term use of the lowest effective dose is generally considered compatible; prefer NSAIDs with established lactation safety where possible.
renal: NSAIDs can reduce renal blood flow and precipitate acute kidney injury, especially in volume depletion, heart failure, or pre-existing renal disease. Avoid in significant renal impairment; if used, monitor renal function closely.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; consider dose reduction. Rare hepatotoxicity can occur - monitor liver enzymes and discontinue if liver injury is suspected.

major: Anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs) and antiplatelets - increased bleeding
Other NSAIDs/aspirin - additive GI and renal toxicity
moderate: ACE inhibitors/ARBs and diuretics (reduced antihypertensive effect, renal risk - 'triple whammy')
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce GI irritation
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - increases risk of gastrointestinal bleeding
interactions.diagnostics: May elevate liver enzymes, BUN/creatinine; can affect bleeding time

monitoring: Renal function (creatinine, BUN) in at-risk patients
Hemoglobin/hematocrit and signs of GI bleeding
counsel: Take with food and a full glass of water
Stop and seek help for black/tarry stools, vomiting blood, or severe stomach pain
Report chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, or slurred speech (heart/stroke warning)
Avoid alcohol and other NSAIDs/aspirin unless advised
Use the lowest dose for the shortest time needed
pk: IR ~6-8 hours; extended-release supports once-daily dosing
Store at 20-25 C; protect from moisture and light
pearls: Boxed warnings: serious cardiovascular thrombotic events and GI bleeding - contraindicated around CABG surgery
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration
Extended-release is not for acute pain due to delayed onset
Watch the renal 'triple whammy' with ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic + NSAID
Avoid in the third trimester of pregnancy
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one - do not take a double dose. For as-needed use, only take it when you actually have pain.
overdose: Overdose may cause drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, GI bleeding, and in severe cases hypotension, respiratory depression, seizures or acute kidney injury. Management is supportive with gastric decontamination if early, fluids, and monitoring of renal function and GI bleeding; there is no specific antidote.
